answer_text:
Let  
\[
N=25!.
\]
First factor \(25!\):

\[
25!=2^{22}3^{10}5^6 7^3 11^2 13\cdot 17\cdot 19\cdot 23.
\]

Since \(p,q\) are relatively prime positive integers and

\[
pq=25!,
\]

no prime can divide both \(p\) and \(q\). Therefore, for each prime power appearing in \(25!\), its entire exponent must go either to \(p\) or to \(q\).

So \(p\) must be a product of some of the full prime-power blocks

\[
2^{22},\;3^{10},\;5^6,\;7^3,\;11^2,\;13,\;17,\;19,\;23,
\]

and \(q\) is the complementary product so that \(pq=25!\).

The condition \(p<q\) means

\[
p<\frac{25!}{p}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p^2<25!.
\]

Since \(25!\) is not a perfect square, equality never occurs, so exactly half of the \(2^9=512\) possible choices for \(p\) satisfy \(p<q\).

Thus the complete set of rational numbers is

\[
\boxed{
\left\{
\frac{A}{25!/A}
\;:\;
A=\prod_{x\in B}x,\;
B\subseteq\{2^{22},3^{10},5^6,7^3,11^2,13,17,19,23\},\;
A<25!/A
\right\}
}
\]

There are

\[
\boxed{256}
\]

such rational numbers.
